figures.caption: Table 1: Comprehensive comparison across four complementary dimensions: (a) NLP fidelity, measuring lexical overlap with reference reports; (b) clinical correctness, evaluating pathology consistency and clinical relevance; (c) diversity and template conformity, quantifying lexical richness and tendency toward template generation; and (d) prevalence-stratified survival, assessing robustness on rare versus common pathologies. Survrare and Survcommon denote recall on the rarest and most common pathology quartiles, respectively, and ∆ measures the performance gap between them. Values are reported across three runs unless otherwise noted. (CRG = Clinical Report Generation score; NBS = Normal Bias Similarity; effVn = 2Hn denotes effective n-gram vocabulary size (single run, deterministic given the model output corpus).)
Figure 3: LLM-as-a-judge Evaluation. VLM baselines (grey bars) score highly on Radiology Style but drop sharply in clinical evaluation, while CLarGen (blue bars) remains high across all metrics.

Figure 1: Template Collapse in 3D CT report generation. (a) Generated reports from VLM baselines form compact clusters in report-embedding space, indicating that many scans are mapped to a small set of semantically similar templates rather than patient-specific descriptions. The color-coded text shows that CLarGen preserves pathology-specific findings aligned with the ground-truth report, while baselines produce generic descriptions with limited findings. (b) Left: cumulative report coverage as a function of the number of unique templates further confirms that a few repeated report patterns (Appendix A.5.1) account for a large fraction of baseline outputs. Right: this produces a clinical bias: common findings are over-reported, while rare but critical pathologies are frequently missed. CLarGen mitigates these effects, producing a broader report distribution and maintaining detection performance across findings of varying prevalence.
